name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q01 - Units of rate constant for reaction orders

questiontext.text:
Match the reaction orders in Column I with the corresponding SI units of rate constant \(k\) in Column II:

Column I (Order)Column II (Units of \(k\))
(A) Zero order(i) \(\mathrm{s}^{-1}\)
(B) First order(ii) \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)
(C) Second order(iii) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\)
(D) Half order (\(n = 1/2\))(iv) \(\mathrm{mol^{1/2}\ L^{-1/2}\ s^{-1}}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
For a general \(n^{\text{th}}\)-order reaction, \(\text{Rate} = k[\text{Concentration}]^n\). Thus, the units of the rate constant \(k\) are given by: \[\text{Units of } k = \frac{\text{concentration}}{\text{time}} \times \frac{1}{(\text{concentration})^n} = (\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^{1-n}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\]

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- For a zero-order reaction (\(n = 0\)): \((\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^{1-0}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1} = \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).
- For a first-order reaction (\(n = 1\)): \((\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^{1-1}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1} = \mathrm{s}^{-1}\).
- For a second-order reaction (\(n = 2\)): \((\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^{1-2}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1} = \mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\).
- For a half-order reaction (\(n = 1/2\)): \((\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^{1-1/2}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1} = \mathrm{mol^{1/2}\ L^{-1/2}\ s^{-1}}\).

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Zero order pairs with \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\), first order pairs with \(\mathrm{s}^{-1}\), second order pairs with \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\), and half order pairs with \(\mathrm{mol^{1/2}\ L^{-1/2}\ s^{-1}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q02 - Classification of reactions by kinetic speed

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical/nuclear processes in Column I with their kinetic characteristics in Column II:

Column I (Process)Column II (Kinetic Characteristic)
(A) Precipitation of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) from \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3(\mathrm{aq})\) and \(\mathrm{NaCl}(\mathrm{aq})\)(i) Very slow reaction
(B) Rusting of iron in air and moisture(ii) Instantaneous ionic reaction
(C) Inversion of cane sugar(iii) First-order radioactive decay
(D) Decay of \(^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}\)(iv) Moderate-speed pseudo first-order reaction

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Chemical and nuclear processes proceed over vastly different timescales, ranging from instantaneous ionic reactions to extremely slow processes.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- Mixing aqueous solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride precipitates silver chloride instantaneously, which is characteristic of fast ionic reactions.
- Rusting of iron in the presence of air and moisture takes a very long time and is a very slow reaction.
- Inversion of cane sugar proceeds at a moderate speed and behaves as a pseudo first-order reaction because water is present in large excess.
- All natural and artificial radioactive decays of unstable nuclei, such as \(^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}\), follow first-order kinetics.

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Precipitation of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) is an instantaneous ionic reaction, rusting of iron is a very slow reaction, inversion of cane sugar is a moderate-speed pseudo first-order reaction, and decay of \(^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}\) is a first-order radioactive decay.

questiontext.text:
Match the kinetic terms in Column I with their correct definitions in Column II:

Column I (Term)Column II (Definition)
(A) Rate law(i) Slowest step in a complex reaction mechanism
(B) Order of reaction(ii) Sum of powers of reactant concentrations in the rate law
(C) Molecularity(iii) Number of reacting species colliding simultaneously in an elementary step
(D) Rate-determining step(iv) Expression relating reaction rate to molar concentrations of reactants raised to experimental powers

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Chemical kinetics distinguishes between experimental rate expressions and mechanistic step counts.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- Rate law is the expression in which reaction rate is given in terms of molar concentrations of reactants with each term raised to some experimental power.
- Order of a reaction is the sum of powers of the concentration of reactants in the rate law expression.
- Molecularity is the number of reacting species (atoms, ions, or molecules) taking part in an elementary reaction that must collide simultaneously.
- The rate-determining step is the slowest step in a complex reaction mechanism that controls the overall reaction rate.

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Rate law matches the experimental concentration-rate expression, order matches the sum of concentration powers, molecularity matches the count of simultaneously colliding species in an elementary step, and rate-determining step matches the slowest step in a complex mechanism.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q04 - Integrated rate laws and linear plots

questiontext.text:
For a reaction \(\mathrm{R} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\), match the kinetic relations in Column I with their corresponding mathematical forms or linear plots in Column II:

Column I (Kinetic Feature)Column II (Expression / Plot)
(A) Zero-order integrated rate law(i) \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\)
(B) First-order integrated rate law(ii) \([\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\)
(C) Zero-order straight-line plot(iii) \(kt = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - [\mathrm{R}]\)
(D) First-order straight-line plot(iv) \(kt = \ln\left(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\right)\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Integrating the differential rate equations for zero-order and first-order reactions yields linear relationships between concentration (or its logarithm) and time.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- For a zero-order reaction, \(-\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{R}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k\), which integrates to \([\mathrm{R}] = -kt + [\mathrm{R}]_0\), or \(kt = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - [\mathrm{R}]\). Therefore, a plot of \([\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\) gives a straight line with slope \(-k\).
- For a first-order reaction, \(-\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{R}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k[\mathrm{R}]\), which integrates to \(\ln[\mathrm{R}] = -kt + \ln[\mathrm{R}]_0\), or \(kt = \ln\left(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\right)\). Therefore, a plot of \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\) gives a straight line with slope \(-k\).

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Zero-order integrated rate law pairs with \(kt = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - [\mathrm{R}]\), first-order integrated rate law pairs with \(kt = \ln\left(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\right)\), zero-order straight-line plot pairs with \([\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\), and first-order straight-line plot pairs with \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\).

questiontext.text:
Match the kinetic quantities in Column I with their corresponding expressions in Column II:

Column I (Quantity)Column II (Expression)
(A) Half-life (\(t_{1/2}\)) of a zero-order reaction(i) \(\frac{\ln 2}{k}\)
(B) Half-life (\(t_{1/2}\)) of a first-order reaction(ii) \(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2k}\)
(C) Slope of \([\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\) for a zero-order reaction(iii) \(\frac{k}{2.303}\)
(D) Slope of \(\log\left(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\right)\) vs \(t\) for a first-order reaction(iv) \(-k\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Half-life \(t_{1/2}\) is the time in which reactant concentration falls to \(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2}\), and linear plots of integrated rate laws yield slopes directly related to \(k\).

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- For a zero-order reaction, substituting \([\mathrm{R}] = \frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2}\) in \(kt = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - [\mathrm{R}]\) gives \(t_{1/2} = \frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2k}\).
- For a first-order reaction, substituting \([\mathrm{R}] = \frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2}\) in \(kt = \ln\left(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\right)\) gives \(t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k}\).
- Plotting \([\mathrm{R}] = -kt + [\mathrm{R}]_0\) against \(t\) gives a slope of \(-k\).
- Plotting \(\log\left(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\right) = \frac{kt}{2.303}\) against \(t\) gives a slope of \(\frac{k}{2.303}\).

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Zero-order \(t_{1/2}\) pairs with \(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2k}\), first-order \(t_{1/2}\) pairs with \(\frac{\ln 2}{k}\), the slope of \([\mathrm{R}]\) vs \(t\) pairs with \(-k\), and the slope of \(\log\left(\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\right)\) vs \(t\) pairs with \(\frac{k}{2.303}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q06 - Experimental rate laws of specific reactions

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical reactions in Column I with their experimentally determined rate expressions in Column II:

Column I (Reaction)Column II (Rate Law)
(A) \(2\mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g})\)(i) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{NH}_3]^0\)
(B) \(\mathrm{CHCl}_3 + \mathrm{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{CCl}_4 + \mathrm{HCl}\)(ii) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{O}_2]\)
(C) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOC}_2\mathrm{H}_5 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}\)(iii) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOC}_2\mathrm{H}_5]^1[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}]^0\)
(D) \(2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Pt}]{1130\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\) (high pressure)(iv) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{CHCl}_3][\mathrm{Cl}_2]^{1/2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Rate laws must be determined experimentally and the exponents of concentration terms may or may not equal the stoichiometric coefficients.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- For \(2\mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g})\), initial rate data show second-order dependence on \(\mathrm{NO}\) and first-order dependence on \(\mathrm{O}_2\), giving \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{O}_2]\).
- For \(\mathrm{CHCl}_3 + \mathrm{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{CCl}_4 + \mathrm{HCl}\), the experimental rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{CHCl}_3][\mathrm{Cl}_2]^{1/2}\).
- For the hydrolysis of ethyl acetate with excess water, the experimental rate expression is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOC}_2\mathrm{H}_5]^1[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}]^0\).
- For the decomposition of gaseous \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) on a hot platinum surface at high pressure, the surface is saturated, making it zero order: \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{NH}_3]^0\).

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Oxidation of \(\mathrm{NO}\) pairs with \(k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{O}_2]\), chlorination of \(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\) pairs with \(k[\mathrm{CHCl}_3][\mathrm{Cl}_2]^{1/2}\), hydrolysis of ethyl acetate pairs with \(k[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOC}_2\mathrm{H}_5]^1[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}]^0\), and \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) decomposition on Pt pairs with \(k[\mathrm{NH}_3]^0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q07 - Arrhenius equation parameters and plot features

questiontext.text:
Based on the Arrhenius equation \(k = A e^{-E_{\mathrm{a}}/RT}\) and its logarithmic form \(\ln k = -\frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{R}\frac{1}{T} + \ln A\), match the items in Column I with their meanings in Column II:

Column I (Parameter / Feature)Column II (Meaning / Value)
(A) Slope of \(\ln k\) vs \(1/T\) plot(i) Fraction of molecules having kinetic energy \(\ge E_{\mathrm{a}}\)
(B) y-intercept of \(\ln k\) vs \(1/T\) plot(ii) Arrhenius frequency factor
(C) \(e^{-E_{\mathrm{a}}/RT}\)(iii) \(-\frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{R}\)
(D) Pre-exponential factor \(A\)(iv) \(\ln A\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
The Arrhenius equation \(k = A e^{-E_{\mathrm{a}}/RT}\) describes the exponential dependence of the rate constant on temperature and activation energy.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- Taking the natural logarithm gives \(\ln k = -\frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + \ln A\). Comparing with \(y = mx + c\), the slope of \(\ln k\) vs \(1/T\) is \(-\frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{R}\) and the y-intercept is \(\ln A\).
- The Boltzmann factor \(e^{-E_{\mathrm{a}}/RT}\) represents the fraction of molecules possessing kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy \(E_{\mathrm{a}}\).
- \(A\) is the Arrhenius factor or frequency factor, a constant specific to a particular reaction.

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
The slope of \(\ln k\) vs \(1/T\) is \(-\frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{R}\), the y-intercept is \(\ln A\), \(e^{-E_{\mathrm{a}}/RT}\) is the fraction of molecules with energy \(\ge E_{\mathrm{a}}\), and \(A\) is the Arrhenius frequency factor.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q08 - Catalyst inhibitor activated complex and threshold energy

questiontext.text:
Match the terms in Column I with their correct descriptions in Column II:

Column I (Term)Column II (Description)
(A) Catalyst(i) Substance that reduces the rate of a reaction
(B) Inhibitor(ii) Activation energy plus energy possessed by reacting species
(C) Activated complex(iii) Unstable transitory intermediate at the potential energy peak
(D) Threshold energy(iv) Lowers activation energy without altering \(\Delta G\) or equilibrium constant

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Reaction rates are influenced by catalysts, inhibitors, and the energetic barrier separating reactants from products.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- A catalyst increases the rate by lowering activation energy along an alternate pathway, without altering \(\Delta G\) or the equilibrium constant.
- An inhibitor is a substance added to reduce the rate of a reaction.
- An activated complex is the unstable, short-lived intermediate formed at the peak of the potential energy barrier before decomposing into products.
- Threshold energy is defined as the sum of activation energy and the energy already possessed by the reacting species.

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Catalyst lowers activation energy without altering \(\Delta G\) or equilibrium constant, inhibitor reduces reaction rate, activated complex is the unstable transitory intermediate at the energy peak, and threshold energy equals activation energy plus reactant energy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q09 - Overall order from rate law expressions

questiontext.text:
Match the rate law expressions in Column I with their overall reaction orders in Column II:

Column I (Rate Expression)Column II (Overall Order)
(A) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{1/2}[\mathrm{B}]^{3/2}\)(i) \(1\)
(B) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{3/2}[\mathrm{B}]^{-1}\)(ii) \(2\)
(C) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}]^{3/2}\)(iii) \(1/2\)
(D) \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Cl}]\)(iv) \(3/2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
For a rate law \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\), the overall order of the reaction is the sum of the exponents: \(n = x + y\).

Step 2 - Step-by-Step Working:
- For \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{1/2}[\mathrm{B}]^{3/2}\): overall order \(= \frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{2} = 2\).
- For \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^{3/2}[\mathrm{B}]^{-1}\): overall order \(= \frac{3}{2} + (-1) = \frac{1}{2}\).
- For \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}]^{3/2}\): overall order \(= \frac{3}{2}\).
- For \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Cl}]^1\): overall order \(= 1\).

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
\(k[\mathrm{A}]^{1/2}[\mathrm{B}]^{3/2}\) has order \(2\), \(k[\mathrm{A}]^{3/2}[\mathrm{B}]^{-1}\) has order \(1/2\), \(k[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}]^{3/2}\) has order \(3/2\), and \(k[\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Cl}]\) has order \(1\).

questiontext.text:
Match the elementary reactions in Column I with their molecularity and mechanistic descriptions in Column II:

Column I (Elementary Reaction)Column II (Molecularity / Description)
(A) \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{NO}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{N}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)(i) Trimolecular (molecularity \(= 3\))
(B) \(2\mathrm{HI} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 + \mathrm{I}_2\)(ii) Unimolecular (molecularity \(= 1\))
(C) \(2\mathrm{NO} + \mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO}_2\)(iii) Bimolecular dissociation of neutral molecules (molecularity \(= 2\))
(D) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + \mathrm{I}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{IO}^-\)(iv) Bimolecular step forming intermediate \(\mathrm{IO}^-\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Molecularity is the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction that must collide simultaneously.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- Decomposition of \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{NO}_2\) involves one reacting species, so it is unimolecular (molecularity \(= 1\)).
- Dissociation of \(2\mathrm{HI}\) involves simultaneous collision of two \(\mathrm{HI}\) molecules, making it a bimolecular reaction of neutral molecules (molecularity \(= 2\)).
- Reaction \(2\mathrm{NO} + \mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO}_2\) involves simultaneous collision of three molecules, so it is trimolecular (molecularity \(= 3\)).
- The step \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + \mathrm{I}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{IO}^-\) is the slow bimolecular elementary step in iodide-catalysed \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) decomposition that produces the intermediate \(\mathrm{IO}^-\).

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
\(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{NO}_2\) decomposition is unimolecular, \(2\mathrm{HI}\) dissociation is bimolecular between neutral molecules, \(2\mathrm{NO} + \mathrm{O}_2\) is trimolecular, and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + \mathrm{I}^-\) is a bimolecular step forming intermediate \(\mathrm{IO}^-\).

questiontext.text:
Match the balanced chemical reactions in Column I with their valid rate expressions in Column II:

Column I (Reaction)Column II (Rate Relation)
(A) \(\mathrm{Hg}(\mathrm{l}) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{HgCl}_2(\mathrm{s})\)(i) \(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5]}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{4}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO}_2]}{\Delta t}\)
(B) \(2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g})\)(ii) \(-\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{Hg}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta[\mathrm{HgCl}_2]}{\Delta t}\)
(C) \(2\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g})\)(iii) \(-\frac{1}{5}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{Br}^-]}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{3}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{Br}_2]}{\Delta t}\)
(D) \(5\mathrm{Br}^- + \mathrm{BrO}_3^- + 6\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Br}_2 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)(iv) \(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{HI}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta[\mathrm{I}_2]}{\Delta t}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
To express the overall rate of a reaction uniquely, the rate of disappearance of each reactant (with a minus sign) and the rate of appearance of each product (with a plus sign) is divided by its respective stoichiometric coefficient.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- For \(\mathrm{Hg} + \mathrm{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{HgCl}_2\), all stoichiometric coefficients are \(1\), so \(-\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{Hg}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta[\mathrm{HgCl}_2]}{\Delta t}\).
- For \(2\mathrm{HI} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2 + \mathrm{I}_2\), dividing by stoichiometric coefficients gives \(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{HI}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta[\mathrm{I}_2]}{\Delta t}\).
- For \(2\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5 \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\), dividing by \(2\) and \(4\) gives \(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5]}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{4}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{NO}_2]}{\Delta t}\).
- For \(5\mathrm{Br}^- + \mathrm{BrO}_3^- + 6\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Br}_2 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), dividing by \(5\) and \(3\) gives \(-\frac{1}{5}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{Br}^-]}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{3}\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{Br}_2]}{\Delta t}\).

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Each reaction pairs directly with the rate expression obtained by dividing \(\Delta[\text{species}]/\Delta t\) by its stoichiometric coefficient.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q12 - First order completion times in terms of half-life

questiontext.text:
For a first-order reaction, match the percentage completion in Column I with the time required in terms of half-life \(t_{1/2}\) in Column II:

Column I (% Completion)Column II (Time Required)
(A) \(50\%\) completion(i) \(\approx 3.32\ t_{1/2}\)
(B) \(75\%\) completion(ii) \(1\ t_{1/2}\)
(C) \(90\%\) completion(iii) \(\approx 10\ t_{1/2}\)
(D) \(99.9\%\) completion(iv) \(2\ t_{1/2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Given Data and Conditions:
For a first-order reaction, \(t = \frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\) and \(t_{1/2} = \frac{2.303}{k}\log 2 = \frac{0.693}{k}\).

Step 2 - Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Dividing \(t\) by \(t_{1/2}\) eliminates \(k\): \[\frac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{\log\left([\mathrm{R}]_0 / [\mathrm{R}]\right)}{\log 2} = \frac{\log\left([\mathrm{R}]_0 / [\mathrm{R}]\right)}{0.3010}\]

Step 3 - Step-by-Step Working:
- At \(50\%\) completion, \([\mathrm{R}] = 0.5[\mathrm{R}]_0\): \(t = t_{1/2}\).
- At \(75\%\) completion, \([\mathrm{R}] = 0.25[\mathrm{R}]_0 = \frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{4}\): \(\frac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{\log 4}{\log 2} = 2 \implies t = 2\ t_{1/2}\).
- At \(90\%\) completion, \([\mathrm{R}] = 0.1[\mathrm{R}]_0 = \frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{10}\): \(\frac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{\log 10}{0.3010} = \frac{1}{0.3010} \approx 3.32 \implies t \approx 3.32\ t_{1/2}\).
- At \(99.9\%\) completion, \([\mathrm{R}] = 0.001[\mathrm{R}]_0 = 10^{-3}[\mathrm{R}]_0\): \(\frac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{\log 10^3}{0.3010} = \frac{3}{0.3010} \approx 10 \implies t \approx 10\ t_{1/2}\).

Step 4 - Check and Final Answer:
\(50\%\) takes \(1\ t_{1/2}\), \(75\%\) takes \(2\ t_{1/2}\), \(90\%\) takes \(\approx 3.32\ t_{1/2}\), and \(99.9\%\) takes \(\approx 10\ t_{1/2}\).

questiontext.text:
For ideal gas-phase reactions carried out at constant volume and temperature starting with initial reactant pressure \(p_{\mathrm{i}}\) and total pressure \(p_{\mathrm{t}}\) at time \(t\), match the reactions in Column I with the reactant partial pressure (or total pressure behaviour) at time \(t\) in Column II:

Column I (Gas-Phase Reaction)Column II (Partial Pressure of Reactant / Behaviour)
(A) \(\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{B}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})\)(i) \(3p_{\mathrm{i}} - 2p_{\mathrm{t}}\)
(B) \(2\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g})\)(ii) \(2p_{\mathrm{i}} - p_{\mathrm{t}}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})\)(iii) Total pressure remains constant (\(p_{\mathrm{t}} = p_{\mathrm{i}}\))
(D) \(\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{B}(\mathrm{g})\)(iv) \(\frac{3p_{\mathrm{i}} - p_{\mathrm{t}}}{2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
At constant volume and temperature, the partial pressure of each gas is directly proportional to its number of moles, and total pressure \(p_{\mathrm{t}}\) equals the sum of partial pressures of all gaseous species.

Step 2 - Step-by-Step Working:
- For \(\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{B}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})\): If pressure of \(\mathrm{A}\) decreases by \(x\), then \(p_{\mathrm{A}} = p_{\mathrm{i}} - x\), \(p_{\mathrm{B}} = x\), \(p_{\mathrm{C}} = x\). Thus \(p_{\mathrm{t}} = p_{\mathrm{i}} + x \implies x = p_{\mathrm{t}} - p_{\mathrm{i}}\), giving \(p_{\mathrm{A}} = 2p_{\mathrm{i}} - p_{\mathrm{t}}\).
- For \(2\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g})\): If pressure of \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5\) decreases by \(2x\), \(p_{\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4} = 2x\) and \(p_{\mathrm{O}_2} = x\). Thus \(p_{\mathrm{t}} = (p_{\mathrm{i}} - 2x) + 2x + x = p_{\mathrm{i}} + x \implies x = p_{\mathrm{t}} - p_{\mathrm{i}}\), giving \(p_{\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5} = p_{\mathrm{i}} - 2(p_{\mathrm{t}} - p_{\mathrm{i}}) = 3p_{\mathrm{i}} - 2p_{\mathrm{t}}\).
- For \(\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})\): If pressure of \(\mathrm{A}\) decreases by \(x\), \(p_{\mathrm{B}} = 2x\) and \(p_{\mathrm{C}} = x\). Thus \(p_{\mathrm{t}} = (p_{\mathrm{i}} - x) + 2x + x = p_{\mathrm{i}} + 2x \implies x = \frac{p_{\mathrm{t}} - p_{\mathrm{i}}}{2}\), giving \(p_{\mathrm{A}} = p_{\mathrm{i}} - \frac{p_{\mathrm{t}} - p_{\mathrm{i}}}{2} = \frac{3p_{\mathrm{i}} - p_{\mathrm{t}}}{2}\).
- For \(\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{B}(\mathrm{g})\): \(p_{\mathrm{t}} = (p_{\mathrm{i}} - x) + x = p_{\mathrm{i}}\), so total pressure remains constant.

Step 3 - Check and Final Answer:
At \(t = 0\), \(p_{\mathrm{t}} = p_{\mathrm{i}}\) reduces each expression to \(p_{\mathrm{i}}\), confirming the algebraic derivations.

questiontext.text:
Match the first-order kinetic problems in Column I with their calculated numerical values in Column II (take \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(\log 2 = 0.3010\)):

Column I (Problem)Column II (Calculated Value)
(A) Half-life when \(k = 5.5 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\)(i) \(1.925 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\)
(B) Rate constant when \(t_{1/2} = 60\ \mathrm{min}\)(ii) \(1.26 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s}\)
(C) Activation energy when rate doubles from \(298\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(308\ \mathrm{K}\)(iii) \(239.3\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
(D) Activation energy for \(\log k = 14.34 - \frac{1.25 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{K}}{T}\)(iv) \(52.9\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Relevant Formulae and Principles:
- First-order half-life: \(t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}\).
- Arrhenius two-temperature equation: \(\log\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 R}\left[\frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\).
- Logarithmic Arrhenius form: \(\log k = \log A - \frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 R T}\).

Step 2 - Step-by-Step Working:
1. For \(k = 5.5 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\): \[t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{5.5 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}} = 1.26 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s}\] 2. For \(t_{1/2} = 60\ \mathrm{min} = 3600\ \mathrm{s}\): \[k = \frac{0.693}{3600\ \mathrm{s}} = 1.925 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\] 3. When rate doubles from \(298\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(308\ \mathrm{K}\): \[\log 2 = \frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left(\frac{10}{298 \times 308}\right) \implies E_{\mathrm{a}} = \frac{0.3010 \times 19.147 \times 91784}{10} \approx 52897\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}} \approx 52.9\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\] 4. From \(\log k = 14.34 - \frac{1.25 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{K}}{T}\): \[\frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 R} = 1.25 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{K} \implies E_{\mathrm{a}} = 1.25 \times 10^4 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \approx 239339\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}} \approx 239.3\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\]

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Each kinetic problem matches its exact calculated value with consistent units.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALKINETICS_MATCH_Q15 - Collision theory and energy distribution concepts

questiontext.text:
Match the collision theory and energy distribution terms in Column I with their correct descriptions in Column II:

Column I (Term)Column II (Description)
(A) Collision frequency (\(Z_{\mathrm{AB}}\))(i) Kinetic energy possessed by the maximum fraction of molecules
(B) Steric factor (\(P\))(ii) Number of collisions per second per unit volume of reaction mixture
(C) Most probable kinetic energy(iii) Collision with sufficient kinetic energy and proper orientation forming products
(D) Effective collision(iv) Probability factor accounting for proper spatial orientation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1 - Conceptual Principle:
Collision theory modifies the Arrhenius rate expression to \(\text{Rate} = P Z_{\mathrm{AB}} e^{-E_{\mathrm{a}}/RT}\), combining collision frequency, activation energy, and molecular orientation, while Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics describe molecular kinetic energy distributions.

Step 2 - Evaluation of Each Pairing:
- Collision frequency (\(Z_{\mathrm{AB}}\)) is the number of collisions occurring per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture.
- The steric or probability factor (\(P\)) accounts for the requirement that colliding molecules must be properly oriented.
- The peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve corresponds to the most probable kinetic energy, which is the kinetic energy of the maximum fraction of molecules.
- An effective collision is one in which molecules collide with sufficient kinetic energy (threshold energy) and proper orientation to break existing bonds and form products.

Step 3 - Final Conclusion:
Collision frequency pairs with collisions per second per unit volume, steric factor pairs with the orientation probability factor, most probable kinetic energy pairs with the energy of the maximum fraction of molecules, and effective collision pairs with a properly oriented collision having sufficient energy to form products.
